newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli leader visits bombed Jewish market.
newsitem.headline: Israeli leader visits bombed Jewish market.

text.p: Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu on Wednesday visited a Jewish marketplace ravaged by a double-suicide bombing, lighting memorial candles to the victims and demanding Palestinian leaders fight "terrorism".

"The fact that the Palestinian Authority has failed to keep its responsibilities to fight terrorism has resulted in this and other tragedies," the prime minister told reporters during a 30-minute solidarity walk through the Mahane Yehuda market.
Netanyahu shook hands with shopowners in the Jerusalem market where a week ago two suicide bombers blew themselves up within seconds of each other, killing 13 other people and wounding 170.
"I think the people of Israel, all of them, support overwhelmingly the firm stance of this government...

"But I think the people in this market -- this market in which we had a terrible massacre -- they are the first to support a firm policy that we expect from the Palestinians to fight terrorism," he said.
Morning shoppers in the market, a stronghold of Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party, chanted his nickname.
"Prime minister, the heavens are crying for those who were murdered," one man shouted.

Netanyahu put on a religious skullcap while lighting a candle and saying a prayer for the dead. Municipal workers and stall owners have been cleaning up and repairing the street market since the blasts.

"The decisive majority of the public in Israel are not ready to accept a one-sided process in which attackers are sent from the territories of the Palestinian Authority or by headquarters there and let it pass quietly. We won't let it pass quietly," Netanyahu said.
Israel demands Yasser Arafat's Palestinian Authority crack down on anti-Israeli militants, and the issue was likely to dominate Netanyahu's talks with Jordanian leaders on Wednesday in Jerusalem.

King Hussein's brother Crown Prince Hassan and Jordanian Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali were due to meet Netanyahu following efforts by Egypt, Israel's first Arab peace partner, to lower tensions in the region in the aftermath of the attack.
While a security stalemate continued between Israel and Arafat's Palestine Liberation Organisation, the military wing of the Islamic militant group Hamas pledged more suicide attacks.
"A chain of martyrdom attacks will come at the appropriate time to hit deep into Zionism," the Izz el-Deen al-Qassam Brigades said in a statement faxed to Reuters in Jerusalem on Tuesday.

The fundamentalist Moslem Shi'ite group Hizbollah, which on Tuesday buried five guerrillas killed by Israeli commandos in south Lebanon, threatened "explosions and suicide bombings" inside "Palestine and...occupied land".
Israel closed the West Bank and Gaza after the twin bombing, stopping tens of thousands of Arab workers from reaching their jobs in Israel, paralysing trade and shutting down factories.
Palestinians have said the Israeli measures are collective punishments that weaken Arafat and strengthen extremist forces.
